projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Inez Wilkinson Harris was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: My name is Douglas Clanin, and I'm an editor with the Indiana Historical Society in Indianapolis. I'm in the home of Mrs. Inez. Her maiden name was Wilkinson. Harris lives on the south side of Anderson, Indiana. I'm making this recording on March 26, 1995, at about 3:20 p.m. I'm in Mrs. Harris' home to discuss aspects of her life and career, primarily when she worked at Delco Remy division from 1926 to approximately 1966, including the war years in World War II. Mrs. Harris, where and when were you born?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I was born in Indiana in 1906.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And you were born in Old Henry County?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And you were born October the 2nd?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Is that correct, ma'am?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And what were the names of your parents?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Anna Wilkinson and Albert Wilkinson, which they always called dad "Bert."

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And how many brothers and sisters did you have and do you have today?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I have one brother and two sisters living, and I've got two sisters dead.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: When you were growing up, what were your parents' principal occupations? What did they do for a living?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: We were big farmers -- I mean, little farmers. It was out in the country. We was born and raised there and lived there till -- well, we went to Shirley. We went to Shirley in 19 -- we lived in Shirley in 1926 when I graduated from Kennard High School. So then after we moved to town and we moved into a great big building. And they called it "The Clubhouse" at Shirley, Indiana. And there was a big stairway going up. And when we come into out of the country into town and there was a big stairway going up. And on each side there was three great big rooms up there. And it was for people could take -- oh, people that worked at the -- see, there was a house there in Shirley where they worked. That's why they had the -- people had that big building.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: And so then we moved there when we left the country. We came out and we lived there. And so I was still just going -- starting into high school when we went in there. And my uncle -- no, my cousin -- that would be awful -- my cousin. We got a chance -- me and my girlfriend got a chance to go to Delco Remy. And so we didn't have no way to go, so I asked my cousin that stayed with us in one of those rooms up there if he'd take us over to Delco Remy. He said he would. So the next morning we took off for Anderson. And then dad and his friend and their family they come to Shirley. And then they walked one of the places there in town where they had -- well, you could get beer there, but also they had -- it was something else. You could go in there, and I forgot where that was. That's been a long time ago. I wish I could thought of -- I wish you would have asked me ahead of time. I could have thought maybe better.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But you guys graduated from Kennard High School in 1926 and then immediately went to start working almost immediately for Delco Remy Anderson?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I sure did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Do you recall what plant that you started at working in?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, Plant 4.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You started in Plant 4?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Plant 4.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, what did they make out there in Plant 4 in those days?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Armatures.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: They made armatures?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: For old-time General Motors armatures?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, did you work on the armature line?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I worked on the armature line.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, what would that entail? What was your job specifically?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I would put wires. The wires had to be put into them. Connect -- had to connect the wires into the round thing on this side because the other part was over here. So we had to put those wires and connect them in that and then cut it off of the whatever you had to work with, you know.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did you kind of have to weave them together, pull the wires over and --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You just -- yeah. They was all standing up and then you had to pull that wire and go around the what-you-call and fill them up and crack the head on them. Had I got a little one in there?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So what we're looking at is a small version of what you worked on in armature?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. You see these things here?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: We had to put -- we had to take our pliers, put them through there and put that down in there and chop it off on the thing all the way down till we got them done. Oh, they was great big ones.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, how long did they give you to bank one of these or assemble one of these?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, the men up here at the front they done them and put the wires in them and put all the stuff in. Then they put them down the line, and us girls had to take them and put them things in there like them are.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Wow. How many hours a day did you work doing that when you first started out?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: We worked eight hours.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Worked eight hours?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, was it -- did you get any kind of breaks at all?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You got a break. They had a hospital there. Oh, yeah. We had the hospital and all kinds of breaks which if you had to go, you had to go.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: We had so many to make, I forget how many we had to make a day.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: That was your rate?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So many during a break?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And was -- do you think the work was difficult or difficult to learn?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: It's harder than purely be darn. It was, really.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Heavy, too.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Do you recall what your initial pay was when you first started?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, Lord. Yeah. I got 18 cents an hour.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: 18 cents?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: When I went in there. And in the three years -- I think it was three years -- I got two or three years I got -- we all did -- a three-cent raise I think it was. I think we got 18 cents and then we got 20 cents -- 21 or something like that after that. And then they kind of just went on. You get a little more every few years.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, all those years you were working there, when did you first have contact with members from the UAW-CIO. When do you recall that they first started talking to you about the union out there?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I don't remember. I'm sorry, Doug, I don't. My mind ain't very good. I remember when they had started that union, but I don't remember. I couldn't tell you what the date was to save my soul.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Do you remember any of the strikes when people would walk out?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, they had them. We lived on -- me and Gibb lived on 27th Street over here, and they had a strike.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Oh, you lived on 27th Street, too?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. And their fence, Delco Remy's fence, was our back fence in our yard.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, let's see. We lived on 613 East 27th Street.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: On down the street then from us, I guess.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And you were down the other direction?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. It was straight west. We went down here to boulevard and turned to the left and we was on that side. We was about one, two, three, four, five -- about five or six houses coming from Columbus Avenue.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay. So --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: On the north side.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: On the north side. So you were closer to Columbus Avenue than we were. We were --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I heard, yeah. We was. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: We're close to, I guess, it's Noble Street.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, Noble Street. No -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Noble Street turns over to 27th.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You were further down into the east of us.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay. But do you remember being out for long periods of time?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: By work you mean?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Back to work?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No, we didn't. Uh-huh. I never.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So the strikes didn't last that long?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No, they didn't. It was hard on some of the people I know, too. But it kind of was on us, too.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And you and Gibb -- we're talking about Gilbert Harris. That's your late husband, now deceased. Now, you were married I think about in 1935 in Cincinnati, Ohio. And did Gibb work out there in Remy?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: He worked at Remy Delco, too.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did he work in the same plant as you did?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. He was in Plant 1. Then he went to another plant.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Of course, we went to Plant 10 when they built the new building over there, you know. I never told you about that. We left there and then we went to Plant 10. A bunch of us did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: And we went into the new building.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So you started out in 4?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: And Gibb went there too in the new building.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: In the new building. And did you meet Gibb over in Plant 10?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. I met him in Shirley. I knew him before we went to work.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you graduate in the same high school class with Gibb?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. No. I went Kennard, and he went to Wilkinson.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay. But they were nearby communities; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. They are just miles apart, you know.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: This short of distance?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Kennard went one way and Wilkinson went the other way. Or was it the other way?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, you worked in Plant 4. When did you move to Plant 10? Do you recall the year that you left Plant 4 and were building those armatures and went to Plant 10?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. That's when I went to work in Plant 4 in '26 when we built those dang armatures. That's what we went in there to do.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: That's where we went the first time I went to work at Remy.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And how long did you stay there?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, until -- well, then I moved. They took a bunch of us people Archie was our foreman; and he took our bunch of us over to Plant 1. And then we did something over there for a while. I don't know what it was till Plant 10 got ready for the rest of us. And then we went to Plant 10. And then when I went over there some, see, some man -- I don't remember now who that was -- one day he come up to me and we was working on -- what were we working on then? In plant -- when I first went to Plant 10. Well, something down the line. What was it now? Anyway, he come up to me one day and he said, "Would you like to" -- see, how did he stay it? "Would you like to do something else?" And I said, "What do you mean?" or something. I don't know. But anyhow he said, "How about you checking the clock cards for everybody? How would you like to work at a desk?" I think that's what he said. And so I said, "Well, what doing?" That's what I said. He said, "Well," he said, "doing the clock cards for your department. Doing the clock cards. Take care of all of them." I did. So I went on the desk then at that time, but I forget when that was or have any idea. I was over in Plant 10, I know.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Was it before World War II started?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, yeah it had to be.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: They opened 10 before World War II.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, they did. It had to be.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But I know that they were heavily involved in the War work then. After the war had started.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, they was.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, I don't know if you could remember this, but a lot of people remember very vividly. Do you remember where you were when you heard the news about Pearl Harbor on December 7th? Do you remember what you were doing that Sunday?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I remember all of us kids were carrying on. I don't even remember what year it was.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: 1941, December 7th.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. In 1941, I guess it was. Well, where would I be in '41? Well, I don't know if I had been in Plant 10 or Plant 4. Can't think of the year.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Do you remember how you felt inside when you heard the news about it?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, we was sick. Everybody was sick. I can't believe I was in Plant 10 then. Everybody was just -- everybody was just -- you just couldn't believe it. It sounded horrible.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: A feeling of shock and --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, man.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: -- disbelief.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, you just couldn't believe it. You couldn't believe it.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And you had to hear it several times before it could finally begin to sink in?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, we did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: A lot of the boys who were already in the service, they didn't even know what Pearl Harbor was.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. That's right. They didn't.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you? When they first said "Pearl Harbor," did you think yourself: Where is that?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: We talked about it. A bunch of us kids talked about that "Pearl Harbor." We didn't have any idea really either.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So you continued to work through the war years?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: The entire time. Yup.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, during World War II, where did you work? Did you have a desk job?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: In 10? Continue on doing that?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, I worked the last over in Plant 10. I forget how many years I was over there though. A mighty long time. I know that's where I ended up at. I don't know. I can't tell you half of what you want to know, I know.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Do you remember how many hours? You worked eight hours before the war, how many hours did you work during the war?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Eight.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, did they -- they ran that plant 24 hours a day, though, didn't they?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. They had second and third shifts.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh. And what shifts did you normally work?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: First always.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You worked the first shift?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, that ran from about what time to what time?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: From -- see, went to work at 7:00 and got off at 3:30.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And then another group would come in to replace you?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Well, not always. Not space. They just -- they had a lot of night forces, but nobody replaced me what I done.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I don't know if anybody did it when we was doing that connector. I don't know. They might have been night people -- I don't know -- on connecting.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: When you say "connecting," what are they connecting?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: That's (indistinct) 'em armatures.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Oh, they moved your armature work over there?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. It was over there, too, some of it. And so was -- then over there in plant -- oh, in the same plant, the new plant, was the people or the girls over in there they done -- they done a lot of winding. I don't know what it was they done, but it was winding -- I know. Coils or something. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Cord winding, probably.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Probably.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: They had the machines to do that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I wish I could thought more -- I had this done a long time ago. You ask now.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you have a desk job throughout the war years or did you also get involved in doing that kind of assembly line work like connecting and winding?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. I was over in Plant 10 when they asked me if I wanted to have a desk job.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: So I went around over there. I forget when that was now, but they just asked me how I'd like to. And I said, "I don't know. What doing?" They said, "Well, taking care of the clock cards in your department." So I stayed with it until I quit.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You did. You stayed with the clock cards, doing that kind of work.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Now, eventually, as war continued on, they needed more and more men, especially to go in the service. And Gibb was called up to active duty in about 1943; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I don't remember, but I'd say about that time.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And he went into Army Air Forces as an aircraft mechanic?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, he got that over there. I don't know what he went in first. I can't tell you.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And he was Fifteenth Air Force, which according to the papers --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, you know what the papers will tell you.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: But I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Was part of the campaign and was aircraft mechanic. And, of course, unfortunately, he's not with us and I didn't ask him the questions about the time to ask him even about those days because he died before I ever got involved in doing these things?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. He had been gone about 16 years. Let's see. He died on Christmas Day of 19 -- it was on Christmas Day. I thought I knew, and I don't really remember anything after that.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: He died -- did he die before my dad did?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. Your dad died I think before Gibb did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay. That's right. He died in January of '81. So Gibb --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Your dad did?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Right. So Gibb then died the following Christmas?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: What year did he?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: '81. 1981. So Gibb probably --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. Gibb died in '82.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay. '82.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: When you said '81, that made me think. He died in 1982 because Mom died in 1979. Did I find that anywhere?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: No, Ed said that.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: She died in '79?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Mom died in '79, and Gibb died in '82.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: On Christmas Day?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Right there almost. He was in bed and George had hollered. Had everybody come in. I had the doors open and everything, placed him up there, and he died up there.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, how did it affect you when he was called to active duty?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, it scared me to death and worried me to death when you are by yourself. It was awful, really, but you had to do it.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you continue to live over there on 27th Street during the war years? Were you down there on 27th Street?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, we was there part of the time. We built our house in '51. I don't know if that tells you anything either. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: That's when we comes over there.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay. So during the war years you'd be over there on 27th Street --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, I'd say so.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: -- primarily.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, did you get involved in wartime activities in terms of -- you know, when they had paper drives, scrap drives, blood drives? They had a lot of --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I didn't. I didn't do that either. No, I didn't do any of that. Uh-uh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: How did rationing affect your life? You know, they had rationing in those days.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, I had other people that they -- we went some place where they had a little bit and somebody else had a little bit of oil or gasoline or something, you know. That is the one you're talking about?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh. Right.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: That's the only one I know. I didn't have any.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you have a car then?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I still had a car, but I never used it. I always went with somebody else and used their gas (laughing). No. They always ask me, you know, to go instead of me going by myself or my car.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you feel it created any hardships for you during those war years, the fact that they had rationing?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, you always had to have somebody to take you someplace to get whatever you wanted. I did. Yeah. But you had to ask somebody. I couldn't go do it.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Were there things that you did without that you really wish you could have gotten access to?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. No. I got along okay.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: No complaints?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Most of the time I was okay.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you try to write Gibb quite often? Did you write to him and did he respond?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, every day. Every day and got one or two back every day too.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So he had time to write and you write to him?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So that probably helped a little bit in terms of the separation?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You ain't kidding. I think all these letters most of them is right in there. I couldn't have put all of them in there. I probably got rid of some of them, but I put the rest of them in there. I got a box just for everything from then and from now on, you know, too.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, I hope those records will be preserved by your nephews.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I do too. Oh, he'll keep that big Bible. It's a big red one. It's that big. And it's -- oh, it's about that thick. It was a beautiful thing. I had all into the middle of it. You could put all that stuff, you know. And that my brother's boy. And he's really -- he's good. He's been to college and everywhere else. And he works still for the Pentagon. But anyway, he's -- he would never part with that thing or hurt it in any way.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I'm glad you have a good home for it.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, I have. That's sure why I give it to him. I + before I got rid of it, too. You know?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Because my brother wouldn't want to do it. And my sister wouldn't do it. I wouldn't let her do it anyway because she's worse than me (laughing).

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you work on Saturdays, too, during the war?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: A few times. Yeah, we had to a few times. Yeah. Not very many people did, but some of us did. If we had to, we did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: When President Roosevelt would have his fireside chats, did you try to listen in on those?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You kidding? We all listened to him. We felt like he was the guy that was gonna really help us. Yeah. Everybody liked him, I thought.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And then when he died --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, that was material.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Really hurt?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, it did. It hurt an awful lot of people at Delco Remy, too. Everyone felt so bad. Yup.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you also read any of the Ernie Pyle columns --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: -- or any other correspondents?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. I seen that Ernie Pyle, read a few things, but I didn't get into it anyway. I'd read some of the paper. I can't think of a dang thing to tell you, to help you out a little more.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You tell me -- there was a funny story that you tell. I don't know if you'll tell us on the tape about the pajama story.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Ha, that was awful. Yeah, that was in nineteen-twenty -- yeah. That was when we went to work out there. Well, Doug, you had to sit -- you was under a -- there you had your bench to work on, you know. Well, you had to cross your feet, had to cross your legs. You wore dresses then when we went to work. And, boy, I tell you by the time I got home bleeding, I was just -- your legs are just killed. If you didn't cross them, everybody coming down the aisle could see up your dress, you know; so I fixed it. I told my girlfriend -- me and her went to work at the same time. I said, "I'm going up and get me some pajamas or something to wear." I didn't want -- we weren't wearing slacks. Nobody was wearing any kind of thing with all our dresses. And, boy, I went to town; and I bought me a new -- let's see. I bought me two new pair, I think it was. One pair was a pretty pajama pair and the other pair was -- well, it was kind of like a pajama, but it wasn't. But they was really beautiful, really pretty things. So I didn't know what I was going to get the first time I went through there, went into Plant 4, me and my girlfriend. And I said, "Oh, Lord." All the men was sitting out here in front of the plant waiting for the whistle to blow. And me and my girlfriend, her name was Gladys Craig. And she didn't get hers then. She said, "Oh, I'll just wait a while." I said, "I ain't going to." I have my legs -- it was a mess. My back hurt. My legs was tired. Anyway, I said, "Look at them guys sitting out there." So they was grinning 'cause they knew because that was the first time anyone had work slacks or any kind of thing to work, pajamas especially. But, oh, they were beautiful. You wouldn't know these was pajamas. You thought they was some kind of a suit or something. But anyway, boy, they just was hollering and yelling. And I was waving at 'em too. I said, "Hi." You know, they was yelling. He said -- they said, "Looks good to us." So in it went. Went right on in. Went in. Went to work. And about 15 minutes later -- I think it was 15 minutes or something like it -- our boss from the line comes up to me. And he said, "They want you in the hospital." I said, "Yeah. What I expect." So I just got up and went in there. And I know dang'on well. I just know that I was going to go home. I just feared they were going to send me home. But, anyway, I went in there. So I'm trying to think who the man, who our big, top man was there in Plant 4. He -- when I went in there, my boss stayed in for a little bit. And when he, the big guy from the front end, went in to the hospital the other guy, the other foreman, left. And when he came in -- I can't think of his name -- and when he come in, he said, "Are you the one that's causing all this trouble?" And I said, "Yeah. I reckon." But I said, "I don't know why." And he said, "Well, why don't you walk around a little bit?" So I did. And he said, "Looks good to me. Why don't you go on out and go to work." Boy, was I tickled. I mean, I was -- really knew I had to go home. I know what he'd tell me. I figured they would too, but they didn't. They would have probably. I don't know. But, of course, they had to get his, I suppose. Oh, Lord. That was a horrible day. Boy, I tell you from then on I never had no dang short dresses on. I tell you that. And didn't either. And then a lot of the other kids started wearing slacks and different things. That was a mean one. They was terrible. Your back was killing you, and you didn't have too much space to cross your legs anyhow. Heck with them.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you ever try that again?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I wore them all the time.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Oh, you wore --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, I sure did. I sure did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Started the trend then?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I forgot the dang dresses, I tell you.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So after that, after a while I suppose the slacks really caught on?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, they did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So you broke the barrier?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I did on that one, buddy. Well, it wasn't because I was hurting. It was crazy anyhow.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Of course, during World War II days that was standard operating procedures. You wore slacks. You see the women in those pictures --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, I know.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: -- coming out of their plants. Rosie the Riveter wearing these overalls.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I know it. That's right.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: A lot more comfortable.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, sure it's comfortable.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Protects your modesty, too.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, it sure did. I never will forget that. I will never forget it.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Oh, one thing I forgot to ask you. You graduated from Kennard High School. You also played on the basketball team, the girls' basketball team.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, I sure did. I played -- well, I had to do the first. What is the -- I don't know what you call in basketball, when you are playing basketball.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You mean the position that you played?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: What were you? Center, forwards, or guard?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. I was at the -- I done that done.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, throw the ball in or the tip-off?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, they put me in as a -- 'cause they said I could run faster than anybody. Which one did I did? Well, there I lost it again, but I knew --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: It might have been the guard if you were the fastest.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. It wasn't no guard.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You were no guard?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. That wasn't that. That wasn't the name of it. No. If I hear it, I remember it. I will tell you. I'll call you or something.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay. You weren't a forward? Were you a forward? I thought you told me --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Maybe that's what it was.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I think you might have told me what it was.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, maybe I did. I think I might have. Maybe I did have it in that piece of paper that I wrote down. Yeah, I believe it was.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You were a forward. Now, how many -- did you play all four years of high school?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. No. We had a new -- they built a new gym. We had a new gym, and the things was up above here. The people sit up there. And, boy, they enjoyed it. And us kids enjoyed it too. We was glad to have that. It was really fun.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: When you were --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Forgot about.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: When your family was involved in farming, what kind of crops did you raise?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, dad just -- he worked for the other fellow. Dad worked for somebody else. And we had corn, and we done cane. I been on the wagon with dad with a big load of cane and took the stuff off them cane and took them to that thing where you have to get the juices, whatever they do.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Oh, sorghum?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Sorghum, yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Sorghum milk, probably.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I did that a lot in the South too because my mother would talk about the sorghum molasses.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: They took the old sorghum milk juice out of there.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yup. Good, though.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you like sorghum molasses?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. We sure did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you put that on cornbread a lot? My grandpa did, the sorghum.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I think dad tried that, but he didn't like it very well. But I heard somebody say he did, but I didn't. I didn't want to put on top of mine. Uh-uh. We had a lot of cornbread and milk -- we did -- out in the country.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So your dad was like a tenant farmer? He worked for the --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: He just worked for somebody else. He never had no farm.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Never had a farm.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: And we moved from one place lots of times. I went to Union Grove School when we was out in the country. That's the name of the place. But you ought to see it today. I wish you could see it today. My cousin just lives by your house from that schoolhouse that we all went to. And we walked. We walked for a mile and a half to school, winter or whatever. And then lots of times my cousins' dad, he'd be coming back from school over there and then us kids would be walking over the school. So he turn around and put us in his buggy and turn around and took us back to our school. I wish you'd see that old schoolhouse today. I'm glad I got it real good before. I got a picture of it. I forget where it is. It's someplace around here.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I think I might have seen that picture.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You wouldn't believe it.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But it has fallen on bad times? It's crumbling?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, it is. And somebody has let somebody have their stuff in there and eat. Cows and stuff and all different stuff. And the walls and stuff, nobody took care of nothing. It looks terrible today. My cousin just lives by from here to there. And she's 80 -- she's 88. And she's all alone. And she's -- I think Liz has seen them. Her sister died about a year and a half ago, which was older than her. And there's just the two of them. Their mom been dead for years. And so they are all humped over. Oh, my. Oh, they got a great big hump on their back. And she can't see, you know, looking up like that. And there she is now all alone. I just feel so bad. I don't know what to do. We herded cows together from one end, from one mile to the other. Her sister -- her older sister -- and my older sister stayed at one end, and me and the other sister then stayed at the other end. When the cows got done, we pushed them back the other end. We made them go back. All we had to do was turn, make them go back, and start eating all the way back again. I've been through the mill, but it was fun.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: That Union Grove School, was that a one-room school?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Had two.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You had two rooms?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: We had two. We had two. I wish you could see that.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, what kind of education -- do you think you got a good education?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, as far as I was concerned. Uh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I've heard positive things.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I got good enough. As long as I graduated, I didn't care. (Laughter.) I just wanted to graduate.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you have any favorite subjects in school, things that you really enjoyed while you were attending either elementary or high school, both? Your favorite subjects that you really, really liked?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, I didn't like history very dang well, I'll tell you. No, I didn't. I liked all the rest of them, but history was hard for me to get through or something. I don't know what it was.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you like to cipher and also reading? Did you enjoy the reading that you did and English?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I liked to read.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But not the history?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. Forget that dang stuff. Let's see. I forgot about some of that stuff.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Were there other sports that you enjoyed besides basketball?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, that's basically -- I like basketball better than anything.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But then later on you did take up golf. When did you start?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Well, that's been probably five, six years ago probably.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Really? You started playing golf five or six years ago?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, I guess you were born in 1906. Five or six years ago that would be about 1988 you took up golf?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I quit playing in nineteen -- let's see. When we went to Florida with Annie and George after Gibb died -- I got someplace when I golf because I had to quit because I got pneumonia down in Florida after Gibb had died.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I remember that.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: And I had an awful time. And I never got over it, so I didn't go back anymore. I think it was '89 when I quit going, when I got that pneumonia.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you play golf mostly in Florida?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. I didn't play but once in Florida. I always played -- me and Annie went to different places. We had that -- we went in down there. Remember that green field where that big place went? Had a big -- oh, where everybody could go into that thing? Hoosierland. Didn't you hear that Hoosierland down there by --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Yes. I heard of that.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, that's where we went, me and Gibb.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: They had a golf course in there?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: They had a golf course. Yeah. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And you liked to play there?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you ever play --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Me and Annie.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: My mom and dad used to go out to Grandview. Did you ever do any golfing out there?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No, I didn't. No golfing out there. Uh-uh. I've been out there, but I never played golf out there.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Yeah? I think that was one of their favorite spots back in the thirties. That's when they played out in the thirties. And that's why mom likes golf today. You like to watch that on TV?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I do, too.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Arnold Palmer?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. We had a -- well, let's see. I can't think. Probably can think of a million more things what I've done. You may not want to hear it. I don't even know now all I've done.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: During -- going back to the war years was there anybody else besides Franklin Delanor Roosevelt that you really admired? Somebody --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, I think I liked all the Presidents, really.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I liked Kennedy. And I liked Bush too. I didn't -- there wasn't anybody that I didn't think -- well, I don't know. Nixon, I liked him. But he still -- I don't know what was wrong with him. I was trying to figure him out, but I couldn't. So --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: A lot of people had that problem, I think.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I know it. It's just something that -- you liked him, but there is just something. I don't know what.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: About him? Was there any war hero or somebody that you really admired, that you remember reading about in the papers or hearings about on the radio that you really admired? Either somebody from this area or elsewhere in the country that kind of stands out besides the presidents?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I expect there is. Probably is. But, Lord, I tell you, Doug, you should have done this about five years ago. See, because it's 6:00 and I can't remember much.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I understand.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: There are lots of things I'll probably remember maybe when you go home, but then I forget that.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: The book I got shows a famous picture out there of Plant 1 when Delco Remy got the Navy -- Army-Navy E. Were you out there that day --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Say what?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: When Delco Remy got the Navy -- Army-Navy E Award for Excellence?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I don't think. I don't know. I don't think I was.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: There's a picture|picket and it shows a lot of people from Delco Remy out there. And it was just Columbus Avenue just packed solid with people when they had the big ceremony to give them the presentation. And I guess that was a big deal in World War II if a plant would get that Army Navy E?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, it would be. But I don't remember. I don't remember doing that. I don't remember that was going on.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I would like to.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Yeah. Do you remember early on during the war, were you aware of when that gas tank blew up over there on the other side of Noble Street, and a lot of people thought the Japanese were attacking?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I remember that, but that's all I know about it. That's the only thing I can remember about that.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, it sure got our attention.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Man, you better believe it did.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: It blew all the windows out of the house. And --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: It did?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Because we were close enough +.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: It may have rattled the windows. I don't know if it broke all the windows, but a lot of people came running out of the house. They thought the Japanese had attacked.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I heard that. I remember that.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I remember the weather was hot, and I think maybe the windows may have been open; but it sure rattled them. And then just a huge fireball and explosion sound. And, boy, just everybody got out ran outdoors.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, I know. That was terrible -- terrible, terrible.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And it was early on during the war where we thought -- we didn't think about the Germans. We thought it was the Japanese.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. I wasn't too sure what was going to happen to the Japanese. I hate that about them two boys and two men over there. They are going to have to be there eight years. That's what I heard today.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: That's what I heard too.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: But you know, Doug, that's awful. Anybody could get lost over there. They didn't have any .

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, they didn't have a border line. You can walk on one side of the sand dune and you're in another country and walk on the other side. And they don't know.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, they ought to be made to fix that so --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Put a line in?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You couldn't get in unless --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: The whole thing ought to be wired down there or something.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Have to be or more people to get that done. That would be awful, wouldn't it?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: That's for sure. During the war, when Gibb was overseas, did you ever feel lonely or were you so busy that you didn't have time to think about that?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. I was pretty lonely. I know what I had to do -- and some lady she stayed with me a little. Oh, I don't know, two or three nights. Wish I could remember her name. No, doesn't do my own.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But she stayed there while Gibb was gone for a period of time?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. And then when he had his back broke and was in the hospital, she come and stayed with me too.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, I didn't know Gibb --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. He had his back broken.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: When did that happen? After the war?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. During the war he fell. His tailbone hit -- his tailbone hooked over the -- he was coming down out of the airplane and he fell and then hit -- his tailbone hit that where you hook on the ladder. With the ladder down there. Yeah. He sure did. That's what ruined him. They had split his back down the middle. Put a -- see, they put one or two. One rod right down through the middle. Well, what am I saying?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: To stiffen his spine? To hold his spine?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. They -- it broke. And then they split his spine right down the middle and put and turned around and put it down vertically. And then they took all these -- a lot of stuff out of his legs and chopped it down in right through, cut down through the middle, chopped that all the way. And then they bolted it back together. He had two bolts in his back when he died.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So they fused it?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: They fused?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Boy, I had no idea.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You could seen them in a picture. You didn't know that?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I forgot. I just happened to think of that.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: No, I had no idea.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: He's had a terrible time since. He could hardly stoop or anything. His back hurt all the time. Didn't think he was ever going to get out of the bed. Didn't think he ever -- boy, it was a horrible thing. Oh, it was awful for him. I forget how long he was in the hospital in Indianapolis.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So he was in the military hospital then?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Like a VA facility?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. He was down in Indianapolis then --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: -- when he had his back split. He done it when he was in Italy. I think it was.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh. But they did have him in the military hospital overseas there for a while?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: For a while.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Then they ended up -- then they finally -- they had to go -- they give him braces. They made him braces. They made him all kinds of different braces, and it didn't do a bit of good. So the doctor told him they just have to have his back sliced in the middle. Yeah. He got two bolts in there, one here and one here. Got to bolt that stuff together to fuse it.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, it was a miracle he was able to walk at any rate.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: He couldn't hardly, but he was straighter than a stick.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: He always was, Gibb was. But that hurt him a little bit. His worry was he just could hardly stoop at all without it killing him.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I had no idea.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: It's awful.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Yeah. Is there anything, Inez, you can remember about your World War II experiences? Anything that stands out in your memory about those years from 1941 to '45? Your work at Remy or anything else that you --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I don't know. I got a lot of diaries in there in the forties.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Oh, you do have diaries. Let me turn this off.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I just really can't think of anything, Doug, that would be interesting. There just a lot of things going on, but I don't know where I was.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But you did get to go to shows once in a while during the war years?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Who was your favorite actor back in those days?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, Lord.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you have a favorite?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. I don't think so. We went to shows. We just watched the show. Well, Clark Gable and someone back _____ was good. We always liked to watch them.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you get to go to dances?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, not while Gibb was gone I didn't. Not even I went a lot.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: What kind of music did you like? Is there a certain band?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah -- no. As long as -- all the crazy or loud things, I didn't like them. I liked good music.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you like Glenn Miller?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And who was that? Russ Morgan?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Of course, now they are bringing the old bands back to the Paramount Theatre again. So you've had a chance to hear the old bands.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I think it's great.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Tommy Dorsey Orchestra even. Some of these old bands come back together.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: My uncle, he played a fiddle down at Shirley.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So you go to dances where your uncle be playing?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. I don't think I ever went when he was playing, but he played a lot. But not only for dances. He worked in a barbershop. He had a barbershop. It was his barbershop. But he had a violin. He always played the violin. He was always playing that. Me and my grandma -- she died from down there. Oh, just everybody seems like.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: When you were out here in Anderson, did you ever go out to the Green Lantern out there in --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: A lot of times.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: A lot of times?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: That was supposed to be quite the place.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah, it was. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And they had a lot of big bands come through there --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. They sure did?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: -- that played?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: We went to a lot, me and Gibb, dancing because they had good dance floors down there. We met a lot of good people, nice people, for years. So things finally just kind of quit, you know, when something happens to somebody. God, I couldn't tell you all, Doug. I'd been better off five or maybe two years ago talking to you. I could remember more.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Well, that's just a kind of natural thing that happens to people.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: It does to people. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: It just --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You know, I guess I never really thought about it until after Gibb was gone. And then I don't know. See, you're by yourself and you don't think. And you do this and you just do what you think what you can do. And you don't think about any other things.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, I think some fellows by the way I've talked to, they think about it a lot 'cause, well, they go out to meet their friends when they go to reunions. One man told me, "I couldn't remember something. I started going to reunions and these fellows would remind me what happened. And this has been 50 years ago." And he said, "If you don't think about it much, there are just certain things you can remember and then everything else you've forgotten."

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You've forgotten.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Then somebody else come along and he can't remember exactly what you remember. So you tell them your little story, and he tells you his story. And you put the two together they --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: -- finally get a better.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Then you get a better idea.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. Maybe ________+.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But if you kept your diaries like you have, you've got complete diaries. You can also go back and look at those diaries.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: If I hadn't -- if I thought I had everything scratched out, I mean, I wouldn't cut them up. Otherwise, I may have cut 'em up before I let anybody have them because I don't know all that I got in them. It ain't funny.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I know. But is there some (doctor?) in the world?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. There'd be a lot of them. But then --

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Very interesting kinds of things.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I know it.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Because on certain date there was a blizzard, but you went to a movie anyway.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yeah. You ain't kidding.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: With your friend "Boots"?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, probably. Yeah, I think it was Boots. She lives in Illinois now.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, this is March, 1944. I think Gibb was in the service, and you weren't going to let a little old blizzard stop you.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: No. Nope.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: You had gone to a show.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: Did you have a favorite movie theater here in town that you liked to go to?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Well, we went to all of them. Every one they had Uptown at that time we went.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: They had the Rivera. They had the Paramount, the State.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Uh-huh. That's about the only ones I know.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I don't know if there was any others.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Those are the ones we went to the most anyway whenever we seemed to relax.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: So now that they fixed you up the old Paramount that brings back a lot of memories?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Man, it does. I'm glad they are doing that. Oh, I'm glad they're doing that. And it's so pretty now. The dance floor is beautiful. I think it's great. I've given -- let's see. I've bought two already. I bought one for Gibb and one for me, our seats. You know, the seats? They was 250 apiece.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And they have a plaque on there with your name?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: I don't know what they are going to do. I don't know how they are going to do it. Don't make any difference. I'm just trying to help. I want to help them to get -- I'd like to have that -- like for them to keep them that way. Get new ones, you know. They are going to get new seats. So that's why.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: And the dance floor, too, upstairs?

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Oh, it's beautiful. Oh, yeah. It's beautiful.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: I would like to see that.

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: Have you been up there?

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: No. I haven't seen the dance floor --

sp.speaker: Inez Wilkinson Harris
sp.p: You've got to go.

sp.speaker: Douglas Clanin
sp.p: But I've seen the Paramount how bad it got. So when they started fixing -- [End of interview audio.]
